## Two philosophies: zone and gap

Every running play in this book is built from the pieces above, and coaches assemble them in two great families. You will
spend a chapter on each; here is the map.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-vs-gap
#| fig-cap: "The two blocking philosophies against the same four-man front, both aimed to the right. Left, zone: every lineman's first step goes the same way (short arrows), each blocks whoever comes into his area, and the running back reads the blocks and picks one of several possible lanes (green dashes). Right, gap (this is the play called power): the play-side linemen block down on the men inside them, the center blocks back, the left guard (purple ring) pulls around to lead up through the hole on the Mike, and the fullback kicks out the end man. The hole is fixed in advance: the C gap, inside the kick-out."
def zg_defense():
    return front([("LE", "9", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)],
                 lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.4, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.8, "M")])


def zone_side(ax):
    off = line("full") + [te(-1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
    p = Play(off, zg_defense(), los=35, to_go=None)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.4, 1.0)])
    p.highlight("RB")
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-7.4, 7.6), window=(-8.4, 6.6), title=False)
    for k in ("U", "LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        q = p.players[k]
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(f, p, 0.1, q.w), _P(f, p, 0.75, q.w + 1.1)
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.5, zorder=6))
    for pts in ([(-1.4, 2.3), (2.6, 2.6)], [(-1.4, 2.3), (0.4, 0.7), (3.0, -0.4)],
                [(-1.4, 2.3), (0.2, 4.6), (2.4, 6.0)]):
        dashed(f, p, pts, color=GREEN, lw=1.4)
    say(f, p, 5.6, 4.6, "the back\nreads the hole", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
    say(f, p, -3.0, -4.6, "everyone steps\nthe same way", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    ax.set_title("Zone: block an area", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


def gap_side(ax):
    off = line("full") + [te(-1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
    p = Play(off, zg_defense(), los=35, to_go=None)
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])                    # down on the 3
    go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.7), via=[(-0.2, 1.4)])                    # up to the backside linebacker
    go_to(p, "C", (0.35, -0.45), via=[(-0.4, -0.2)])                  # back block on the 1
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.1, -2.3), via=[(-0.7, -2.8)])                  # hinge
    go_to(p, "U", (0.2, -5.1), via=[(-0.6, -5.0)])                    # cut off the end
    go_to(p, "LG", (3.7, 2.4), "pull", via=[(-3.05, -1.1), (-3.05, 2.4), (0.3, 3.6)])  # pull, lead up on the Mike
    go_to(p, "FB", (0.3, 3.75), via=[(-1.8, 3.0)], speed=5.0)          # kick out the end
    go_to(p, "RB", (2.6, 3.4), "run", via=[(-4.4, 1.2), (-1.5, 3.0)])
    p.highlight("RB"); p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-7.4, 7.6), window=(-8.4, 6.6), title=False)
    point_to(f, p, (5.6, 5.4), (0.3, 3.8), "fixed hole:\nthe C gap", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, shrink=3)
    say(f, p, -3.0, -4.6, "down blocks,\na puller, a kick-out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    ax.set_title("Gap: block a man, add a blocker", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
zone_side(axes[0]); gap_side(axes[1])
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

**Zone** blocking assigns blockers to *areas*. All the linemen step the same direction at the snap, each takes whoever
enters his area, uncovered men double-team and climb, and the running back reads where the wall cracks. Its virtue is
that it adapts: if the defense slants or blitzes, whoever arrives gets blocked. Its price is that blocks are rarely
knock-down blocks, and the hole is not known in advance, so the play depends on a runner who can see it.
([Zone Running](03-02-zone-running.qmd) is the full story.)

**Gap** blocking (also called *man* or *power* blocking) assigns blockers to *men*, chosen to give them angles, and moves
extra blockers to a hole chosen in advance. Down blocks seal the inside, a kick-out walls off the outside, and a puller or
a fullback leads through the space between them. Its virtue is numbers at the point of attack: it gets more blockers to
the hole than the defense has defenders there. Its price is that it is easier to read (a pulling guard is a signpost) and
more fragile against movement: if a defender slants into the space a puller was supposed to run through, the play can die.
([Gap Schemes](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) covers power, counter, trap and their relatives.)

Neither is better. Almost every NFL team runs both, and good offenses build them to look alike for the first half-second
so the defense cannot tell which is coming. The first thing to watch on any run is which family it belongs to, and you can
usually tell from one question: **does the whole line step the same way, or does somebody pull?**

## Where this language came from: the Hogs

Most of this vocabulary is older than anyone now coaching, but one team made it famous to a national audience, and its
story explains why the blocks in this chapter are still the foundation.

When Joe Gibbs became Washington's head coach in 1981, his offense was built to run behind a big offensive line. Line coach
**Joe Bugel** started calling his linemen "the Hogs" in training camp in 1982 ("Okay, you hogs, let's get running down
there"), and the name stuck to a group of big, unglamorous blockers (center Jeff Bostic, guards Russ Grimm and Mark May,
tackles Joe Jacoby and George Starke, among others) who became the most famous offensive line in football.[^hogs]
Washington won three Super Bowls under Gibbs, after the 1982, 1987 and 1991 seasons, with three different starting
quarterbacks, which tells you how much of the offense lived up front.

Gibbs's teams are a good place to see the language in use because their signature runs were the gap-scheme plays this
chapter just described: down blocks on the play side, guards and even tackles pulling around to kick out and lead, a
fixed hole. Their counter play, with two backside linemen pulling (the left guard Russ Grimm and, unusually, the left
tackle Joe Jacoby), became one of the most copied runs in football (it is taught in [03-03](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)).[^counter] And Gibbs's answer to one defender, the Giants' Lawrence Taylor, gave
the run game a new blocker: Gibbs moved a back up near the line as an extra blocker for the edge, the position now called
the *H-back*.[^hback] That is hat math again. Taylor was a defender the existing blocking could not handle, so Gibbs added
a hat.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Washington, Super Bowl XVII (1982 season)"}
**The play:** January 30, 1983, at the Rose Bowl. Washington trails Miami 17–13 with 10:10 left in the game and faces
fourth-and-1 at the Miami 43. Gibbs calls "I-Right 70 Chip," a short-yardage run to the left. Tight end Clint Didier goes
in motion to the right and then reverses back to the left, and cornerback Don McNeal follows him. The play is designed, as
the standard account of it puts it, to block everyone except the smallest defender on the field, the cornerback, and let
John Riggins run through him. Behind Didier and fullback Otis Wonsley, Riggins breaks McNeal's tackle at the line (McNeal had
slipped as Didier changed direction) and outruns safety Glenn Blackwood for a 43-yard touchdown. Washington wins 27–17;
Riggins carries 38 times for 166 yards and is named MVP.[^sb17]

**What to notice:** this is hat math in its purest form. The offense could not block everybody, so it chose the defender to
leave free: the smallest one, against a 230-pound back with a running start. Watch the replay with the vocabulary: which side
is the play side, which gap Riggins hits, who leads (the fullback), and what the motion did to the cornerback before the snap.
([Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) is about that last idea.)
:::

Five years later the same line produced an even more lopsided day: in Super Bowl XXII, after the 1987 season, rookie
Timmy Smith, making his first career start, ran for 204 yards, still the Super Bowl record, in a 42–10 win over
Denver.[^smith]

The modern echo of the Hogs is not one team but one position. As offenses spread out and defenses got faster, the center
became the hub of the run game: the man who makes the line's calls, who is usually uncovered and must climb, and who in some
offenses pulls. Two recent lines show the vocabulary at its best.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2022"}
**The season:** the 2022 Eagles went 14–3 and reached Super Bowl LVII, which they lost 38–35 to Kansas City. By this book's
calculation from nflverse play-by-play, they were first in the league in both EPA per designed run and success rate on designed
runs, and first in rushing touchdowns on designed runs. Those numbers include Jalen Hurts's designed runs and the Eagles'
short-yardage quarterback sneaks, a reminder from the last section that a quarterback who runs is part of the blocking
arithmetic.[^eagles]

**What to notice:** watch center **Jason Kelce** (#62) on every run for a quarter. Count how often he is the lineman who comes
off a double team and climbs to a linebacker, and how often he pulls or sprints out in front of a play to the edge. Then watch
his guards: on most of the plays where Kelce climbs, a guard is finishing the defensive lineman Kelce left. That is the combo
block, done at a speed most centers cannot match.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Detroit Lions 2023–2024"}
**The seasons:** under offensive coordinator Ben Johnson, Detroit reached the NFC Championship Game after the 2023 season and
went 15–2 in 2024. By the same nflverse calculation, the Lions were in the top five in EPA per designed run in both seasons and
tied for the league lead in rushing touchdowns on designed runs both years.[^lions] Their line was anchored by right tackle **Penei Sewell**
(#58), a first-team All-Pro in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and center **Frank Ragnow** (#77), a second-team All-Pro in 2023 and 2024
who retired in June 2025 (a comeback attempt that November ended when he failed his physical).[^sewell] (Johnson became the Bears' head coach in 2025, so this is a 2023–2024 offense, not
Detroit's current one.)

**What to notice:** pick a game and watch only the right side. Sewell's blocks are a block-library tour: down blocks on runs
to his side, drive blocks that move defensive ends a couple of yards off the ball, reach and cut-off blocks when the play goes
away from him. Then watch Ragnow on the double teams in the middle: who climbs, and when. Name each block out loud as it
happens.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: find the hole.** For one quarter, on every run, do this.

*Before the snap*

- Count the box and the blockers (five linemen, plus each tight end and fullback near the line). Six against six? Seven
  against six? Who would be the free man?
- Read the defensive line in numbers, left to right ("5, 1, 3, 9"). Which guard has a 3-technique on him? Which linemen are
  uncovered?

*The first half-second*

- Watch the running back's **first step**. It points at the play side and usually at the point of attack. Say the gap out
  loud before he gets there: "right B gap."
- Glance at the guards. Does one pull? (Gap play, and the puller is running to the hole.) Does the whole line step together?
  (Zone, and the hole is not decided yet.)

*After the play (on the replay)*

- Name the gap he actually hit. Same as your guess? On a gap play it usually is; on a zone play it often is not, and that is
  the play working, not failing.
- Find one block of each kind you can see: a down block, a double team with a climb, a kick-out, a lead.
- Find the unblocked defender. Where was he, and did he make the tackle?

For your [prediction log](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd): before each run write the gap you expect
(say, "R-B"); afterwards write the gap he hit and Z (zone) or G (gap). After a quarter you will know whether this offense's
first step tells the truth.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. Find the hole.** First-and-10. @fig-drill-1 shows the first half-second of a run: the linemen's first steps, a
pulling guard (purple ring), the fullback heading for the edge, and the running back's first two steps. The defense has a
linebacker (S) standing up on the line outside the tight end. Where is the point of attack (name the gap)? Name the block the
Y and the RT are throwing, and say what the fullback and the pulling guard are about to do.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: the first half-second of a run from the I-formation. The tight end and right tackle have stepped inside, the left guard (purple ring) is pulling to the right, the fullback is heading outside, and the running back has taken two steps to the right."
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("R7", "7", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.4, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.6, "M"), ("SAM", 1.0, 6.9, "S")])
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: the first half-second. Where is it going?")
go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 4.25), via=[(-0.3, 4.55)])                 # down on the 7
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])                 # down on the 3
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.7), via=[(-0.2, 1.4)])                 # up to the Will
go_to(p, "C", (0.35, -0.45), via=[(-0.4, -0.2)])               # back on the 1
go_to(p, "LT", (-0.1, -2.3), via=[(-0.7, -2.8)])               # step inside
go_to(p, "LG", (-1.9, 3.9), "path", via=[(-3.05, -1.1), (-3.05, 3.0)])  # pulls (where to, you decide)
go_to(p, "FB", (-1.3, 6.1), "path", via=[(-3.1, 3.7)], speed=5.0)       # heading for the edge
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.8, 1.7), "run", via=[(-6.0, 0.6)])          # first two steps
p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-8.6, 10.6), window=(-8.4, 7.0))
say(f, p, 3.4, 8.2, "S: standing\nup on the edge", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The D gap, just outside where the tight end lined up.** Everything on the play side is going *inside*: the Y is down-blocking
the 7-technique and the RT is down-blocking the 3-technique, hitting each from the side and sealing the inside of the hole.
That leaves the end man, the S standing up outside the tight end, for the **fullback to kick out**: he will hit him from the
inside and push him toward the sideline. The **pulling left guard** turns up into the space between the down blocks and the
kick-out and **leads** through it onto the first linebacker who shows (here the Mike, flowing over). The running back follows
the puller. Inside the hole: down blocks. Outside it: the kick-out. Through it: a lead. That combination is the play called
*power*, the signature gap-scheme run, and [03-03](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) builds it fully.

The tell you could have used: the back's first steps aimed outside the tackle, and the guard pulled the same way. A zone
run does not pull guards; a pulling guard almost always runs to the hole.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. Count the hats.** Second-and-1. The offense brings in a fullback and lines up in the I-formation with one tight end
(21 personnel); the defense answers with four down linemen, three linebackers and two deep safeties. Do the hat math for a run.
Who is unblocked? If the defense wants to stop the run harder, what will it do, and what does that give the offense?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: second-and-1 (yellow line one yard ahead). 21 personnel in the I-formation against a base defense with two deep safeties. The shaded area is the box."
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", -0.7, -11.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 11.0, "Z")]    # tight splits
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("R7", "9", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.2, "M"), ("SAM", 4.4, 6.4, "S")])
dfn += [D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -11.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 11.0, "CB"),
        D("FS", "S", 12.0, -6.5, "FS"), D("SS", "S", 12.0, 6.5, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=1, title="Drill 2: 2nd and 1, 21 personnel, a base defense")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.8, lateral=(-13.0, 13.0), window=(-8.6, 14.2))
shade_box(f, p, -4.6, 7.4, d1=7.0)
say(f, p, 9.0, 0.0, "the box", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Seven against seven: a hat on every hat.** In the box are seven defenders: four linemen (a 5, a 1, a 3 and a 9) and three
linebackers. The offense has seven blockers: five linemen, the tight end, and the fullback as a lead blocker. Every defender in
the box can be blocked, and the two free defenders are the safeties, twelve yards deep. On second-and-1 that is a very good
look to run into: the runner needs one yard, and nobody unblocked is within ten of him.

**If the defense wants the run more,** it brings a safety down into the box: eight against seven, plus-one again. But that
leaves one deep safety for two receivers and a tight end, and on second-and-1 the offense can afford a shot: play-action, with
the fullback and tight end selling the run, against a single safety. This is the back-and-forth of hat math: the offense adds a
blocker, the defense adds a defender, and whoever over-commits gets punished by the other half of the playbook.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. Read the front.** The defense's linemen are drawn with question marks. Read their alignments as technique numbers,
left to right. Then: which offensive linemen are covered and which are uncovered? If the offense runs an inside run to the
right, where will its double teams most naturally form, and who will climb to the linebackers?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: shotgun, one tight end on the right. Four defensive linemen (marked ?) and two linebackers. The offense will run inside, to the right."
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L3", "3", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -1.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.6, "M")])
dfn = [q.moved(label="?") if q.pos == "DL" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.5, "R")], dfn, los=40,
         to_go=10, title="Drill 3: name the front, then find the double teams")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-8.0, 8.6), window=(-6.6, 7.0))
play_arrow(f, p, 6.2, -2.0, 3.0, "inside run to the right", fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**5, 3, 3, 9.** From the left: a 5-technique on the left tackle's outside shoulder, a 3-technique on the left guard's outside
shoulder, a 3-technique on the right guard's outside shoulder, and a 9 outside the tight end. (Two 3-techniques is a common
modern nickel look: both defensive tackles in the B gaps, ready to penetrate.)

**Covered:** LT (by the 5), LG (by the left 3), RG (by the right 3), Y (by the 9). **Uncovered:** the center and the right
tackle. Those two are the free hats. On an inside run to the right, the natural pair is the **right guard and right tackle on
the right 3-technique**: the RG is covered, the RT is uncovered beside him, so they double-team the 3 and the **RT climbs** to
the Mike. The **center**, uncovered with nobody on him, can help the left guard on the other 3-technique and then climb to the
Will. The Y has the 9 by himself, and on an inside run to the right that is the edge of the play.

Notice what the front did: by putting both tackles in 3-techniques, the defense left the center uncovered, so the center
becomes the climber, which is why NFL offenses prize centers who can move.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Gaps and holes name the spaces.** Gaps are lettered A, B, C, D outward from the center (the defense's language; every gap
  needs a defender, and every blocker the offense attaches to its line adds one). Holes are the offense's numbers, usually odd
  on one side and even on the other, and "24" means the 2-back through the 4 hole, though numbering is a dialect.
- **Technique numbers say where a defender stands:** even numbers head-up (0 center, 2 guard, 4 tackle, 6 tight end), odd
  numbers on an outside shoulder (1, 3, 5, and 9 outside the tight end), "i" on an inside shoulder (2i, 4i), and 7 inside the
  tight end. A shaded defender usually owns the gap he is shaded into; the **3-technique**, **4i** and **5-technique** have
  become names for positions.
- **Covered or uncovered** is the first question every lineman asks. Covered linemen have a man; uncovered linemen are the
  free hats, the ones who double-team and climb.
- **Eight blocks describe almost every run.** Four win a matchup with the best angle available (drive, down, reach, cut-off);
  four change the numbers (combo, pull, kick-out, lead). Play-side blocks make the hole; backside blocks stop pursuit.
- **Hat math decides runs before the snap.** A handoff leaves the quarterback a spectator, so the offense plays ten against
  eleven and the defense has two free men to place, deep or in the box. A quarterback who can run, or a read that "blocks" a
  defender without touching him, gets one back.
- **Zone and gap are the two answers.** Zone blocks areas and lets the runner find the hole; gap blocks men with angles and
  brings extra blockers to a hole chosen in advance. Watch the first step: together, or does someone pull?

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**Hat math in the data, and why it is slippery.** The NFL's participation data, which nflverse publishes, records how many
defenders were in the box at the snap. You might expect runs into seven-man boxes to do clearly worse than runs into six-man
boxes. Here is what 2023–2025 shows for one personnel group in one situation.

```{python}
#| label: box-data
#| output: asis
import re as _re
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

pb = pbp([2023, 2024, 2025], columns=["game_id", "play_id", "season_type", "play_type", "qb_scramble", "qb_kneel",
                                      "qb_spike", "down", "ydstogo", "yardline_100", "wp", "epa", "success",
                                      "yards_gained"])
part = nfl().load_participation([2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting([2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "is_qb_sneak"]]
pb = pb[(pb.season_type == "REG") & pb.play_type.isin(["run", "pass"]) & (pb.qb_kneel == 0) & (pb.qb_spike == 0)]
m = (pb.merge(part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])
       .merge(ftn, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"], how="left"))


def counts(s):
    """'1 C, 2 G, 1 QB, 1 RB, 2 T, 1 TE, 3 WR' -> (backs, tight ends, offensive linemen)."""
    g = {k: int(v) for v, k in _re.findall(r"(\d+) (\w+)", str(s))}
    return g.get("RB", 0) + g.get("FB", 0), g.get("TE", 0), g.get("C", 0) + g.get("G", 0) + g.get("T", 0)


c3 = m["offense_personnel"].map(counts)
m["eleven"] = [c == (1, 1, 5) for c in c3]
s = m[m.eleven & (m.down == 1) & (m.ydstogo == 10) & m.yardline_100.between(20, 80) & m.wp.between(0.2, 0.8)
      & m.defenders_in_box.between(5, 8)].copy()
s["run"] = (s.play_type == "run") & (s.qb_scramble == 0)
runs = s[s.run & (s.is_qb_sneak != True)]
rows = ["| Defenders in the box | Plays | Run share | Runs | Success rate | Yards per carry |",
        "|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
for box, g in s.groupby("defenders_in_box"):
    r = runs[runs.defenders_in_box == box]
    rows.append(f"| {int(box)} | {len(g):,} | {g.run.mean():.0%} | {len(r):,} | {r.success.mean():.0%} | "
                f"{r.yards_gained.mean():.1f} |")
print("\n".join(rows))
```

*Runs and box counts, 2023–2025 regular seasons: 11 personnel (one back, one tight end, five offensive linemen),
first-and-10 between the 20s, win probability 20–80%. Box count is from nflverse participation data (FTN charting);
"run share" counts designed runs (no scrambles or kneels) among runs and passes; success means positive EPA, and
quarterback sneaks are left out of the run columns.*

Two things jump out. Offenses do respond to the count: they ran on a small share of snaps against light boxes, which usually
come with more defenders deep and wide. But the runs that offenses *did* call into seven- and eight-man boxes did not fare
dramatically worse, and the share of plays that are runs goes *up* as the box gets heavier. That is not hat math failing.
It is selection. Box counts are not random: defenses load the box when the offense's formation and tendencies say run, and
offenses that see seven in the box often check out of the weakest runs, so the runs that survive are the ones the offense still
liked. A simple comparison of averages cannot separate the arithmetic from the decisions made around it. That problem, and the
tools for it, are in [Expected Points, EPA and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)
and [Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From diagrams to real tracking data.** The combo-block animation is a gridiron simulation written in NFL Big Data Bowl
coordinates, so real tracking data drops into the same drawing code. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9)
includes every player's position ten times a second, before and after the snap, and its `plays.csv` carries PFF's run-concept
labels, so you can find inside runs and watch a center and guard come off a double team for real. The data needs a free Kaggle
login, so the code (in the web edition, under "Show the Python") is not run when this book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
iz = plays[plays["pff_runConceptPrimary"].astype(str).str.upper().str.contains("INSIDE ZONE")]
g, pl = iz.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.4, 0.85, 1.35])   # the same moments as the simulated combo block
```
